books.section: Topic 3.2 The Seven Years' War (The French and Indian War)

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.
stimulus.text:
| Year | Turning point | What changed |
| 1754 | Seven Years' War begins in North America | Britain and France fight for the continent; the colonies are drawn into an imperial war |
| 1763 | Treaty of Paris ends the war | France loses Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi; Britain takes on a huge war debt |
| 1763 | Proclamation of 1763 | Settlement west of the Appalachians is forbidden; the age of salutary neglect ends |
| 1765–1773 | Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Boston Tea Party | Parliament taxes the colonies for revenue; colonists resist, then organize |
| 1776 | Declaration of Independence | The colonies break with Britain and claim government rests on the consent of the governed |
| 1783 | Treaty of Paris ends the Revolution | Britain recognizes American independence; the new nation holds the land to the Mississippi |
| 1787–1789 | Constitution written and ratified | The weak Articles give way to a stronger federal government |
| 1800 | Election of Thomas Jefferson | Power passes peacefully from one party to another for the first time |

source: original; stimulus is an original data table compiled from the grounding books
stem: According to the table, which event best marks the end of the era when Britain left its colonies largely alone to govern themselves?

options.text: The Seven Years' War begins in 1754, when colonial forces first fight alongside British regulars.
options.misconception: The war itself did not change how Britain governed; the change came after victory.

options.text: The Declaration of Independence in 1776, when the colonies reject British rule entirely.
options.misconception: By 1776 the era of neglect was long over; the break was the result, not the start, of tighter rule.

options.text: The election of 1800, when power passes peacefully between American political parties.
options.misconception: The election of 1800 concerns the American republic, not British rule.

options.text: The Proclamation of 1763, when Britain forbids settlement west of the Appalachians and rules more directly.

rationales.A: The war itself did not change how Britain governed; the change came after victory.
rationales.B: By 1776 the era of neglect was long over; the break was the result, not the start, of tighter rule.
rationales.C: The election of 1800 concerns the American republic, not British rule.
rationales.D: The table places the Proclamation of 1763 right after the Treaty of Paris, and the change it marks is a new kind of British rule. Background: before the war Britain had practiced salutary neglect, leaving the colonies to govern themselves while it looked the other way. The Proclamation was the first of a new series of restrictions — a line drawn by London across the map — and it told the colonists that the old loose arrangement was over.
rationales.general:
1. Find the break in the table. The war ends in 1763, and in the same year Britain draws a line the colonists may not cross.
2. Ask what came before. For decades Britain had left the colonies largely alone — salutary neglect.
3. Ask what the Proclamation did. It was London ruling directly, over land the colonists thought was theirs to settle.
4. Put it together. The Proclamation is the first step on the road from neglect to revolution.
Remember: the end of neglect is not a battle — it is a line on a map drawn in London.
